Neonatal sperm whales enter the world at a remarkable size, with newborns measuring approximately 400 centimeters [Lb = approximately 400 centimeters] in total body length. This substantial birth length is a direct consequence of an extended gestation period, which lasts for about 502 days [tg = about 502 days] under the species' typical core body temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], a value inferred from studies on killer whales. The corresponding wet weight at birth is roughly 1,000,000 grams [Wwb = roughly 1,000,000 grams], representing the heaviest neonates among all cetacean species. This massive investment in a single offspring at parturition reflects a life-history strategy centered on producing a highly precocial calf capable of swimming and diving alongside its mother almost immediately after delivery. The energetic costs of maintaining such a large foetus in utero for over sixteen months are substantial, and pregnant females undergo significant metabolic demands during the later stages of embryogenesis. Comparative data from other large odontocetes suggest that the prolonged gestation period is intimately linked to the development of the calf's sophisticated echolocation apparatus and thick blubber layer, both critical for survival in the deep, cold waters these whales inhabit from birth.

Adult sperm whales exhibit one of the most extreme examples of sexual size dimorphism among all mammals, a pattern readily apparent in their asymptotic body lengths. Mature females typically cease growing upon reaching an ultimate length of approximately 1100 centimeters [Li = approximately 1100 centimeters], whereas adult males continue their somatic growth for many additional years, attaining a far more imposing maximum total length of about 2050 centimeters [Li = about 2050 centimeters]. This pronounced disparity in final body size is mirrored by an equally dramatic difference in ultimate wet weight between the sexes. The largest females, having concluded their growth phase, achieve a maximum recorded body mass of 14,000,000 grams [Wwi = 14,000,000 grams], while the dominant, fully-grown males can tip the scales at an astonishing 57,000,000 grams [Wwi = 57,000,000 grams]. This remarkable sexual dimorphism, particularly the much larger size of males, is generally interpreted in the context of intense male-male competition for access to receptive females. Larger body size confers a decisive advantage in the aggressive physical contests that determine mating success, driving the evolution of this extreme growth trajectory in males, which continues long after females have reached their own adult dimensions.

The reproductive biology of the sperm whale is characterized by an exceptionally slow pace of life, with females displaying a strikingly low maximum reproductive output. In this species, a reproductively active female produces a single calf per reproductive event [N_R_i = single calf per reproductive event], with a frequency of approximately 0.4 reproductive events per year [F_R_i = approximately 0.4 reproductive events per year], all physiological processes occurring at their typical internal temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C]. This unusually long inter-birth interval is among the longest recorded for any cetacean and is a key component of their slow life-history strategy. The extended interval between successive births is necessitated by the prolonged period of maternal dependency, which includes a substantial lactation phase. The nutritional independence of the calf does not occur until approximately 560 days after birth [tx = approximately 560 days after birth], a weaning period that also unfolds under the species' consistent core temperature at a temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C]. This extended period of maternal investment ensures that the calf is sufficiently large and experienced to forage independently in the deep ocean before the mother can allocate energy toward the next reproductive event.

Sexual maturation in sperm whales is a protracted process that occurs at vastly different ages in males and females, consistent with their divergent life-history trajectories. Female sperm whales typically attain puberty, marked by the onset of ovulatory cycles, after a period of about 2,922 days since birth [tp = about 2,922 days since birth], which corresponds to approximately eight years of age, given their core body temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C]. In contrast, males follow a much slower developmental schedule, not reaching sexual maturity until approximately 3,650 days since birth [tp = approximately 3,650 days since birth], or roughly ten years, also at 36 °C [T = 36 °C]. However, this milestone of physiological puberty does not translate into immediate reproductive success for males. Social maturity and the physical size needed to compete for mating access typically require many additional years of growth, often delaying effective breeding until they are well into their twenties. This prolonged period of somatic growth in males is directly linked to their much larger ultimate body size compared to females, as the energy that females channel into reproduction must instead be invested in continued mass gain by males to achieve the size necessary for dominance in future breeding seasons.

The extreme longevity of the sperm whale represents the final piece of its slow-paced life-history puzzle, with individuals capable of surviving for many decades. Field studies and analyses of tooth growth layers have estimated that the maximum recorded lifespan for this species is approximately 77 years [am = approximately 77 years] when maintained at their typical physiological temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C]. This remarkable lifespan is consistent with the pattern observed across other large, long-lived mammals, where delayed maturity and low reproductive rates are coupled with extended survival. The combination of a very late age at first reproduction for males, the exceptionally long 502-day gestation period (502 days) [tg = 502 days], and the investment in a single, well-developed calf every few years means that an individual female can only produce a limited number of offspring over her entire lifetime at a temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C]. This low reproductive output, together with the protracted period until weaning at 560 days after birth [tx = 560 days after birth], renders sperm whale populations exceptionally vulnerable to anthropogenic threats such as ship strikes and entanglement, as any reduction in adult survival has a disproportionately large impact on population growth rates at a temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C]. Consequently, the conservation of this species relies heavily on protecting individuals across all age classes to maintain the demographic stability of these deep-diving leviathans.
